overview: This file documents the U.S. diplomatic response to Japanese regulations introduced in July 1941 restricting the languages permitted in domestic and international telephone conversations and telegrams. The restrictions prevented American diplomatic and consular personnel from using English for calls within the Japanese Empire, prompting inquiries about precedent, arguments based on reciprocity, and a formal protest by Ambassador Joseph C. Grew. The correspondence also records Japan’s claim that its policy answered similar British measures, the British Foreign Office’s emphatic denial of that claim, and continued U.S. pressure for a formal response. Although the principal despatch is dated August 19, subsequent telegrams trace the dispute through September 19, when the Japanese Foreign Office announced that foreign-language telephone conversations had again been permitted.

subfiles.title: Telegram from Grew reporting Japanese language restrictions
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador in Japan
subfiles.about: Reports new Japanese restrictions on the languages permitted in telephone and telegraph communications.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports that regulations effective July 12 generally require Japanese for telephone calls within the Japanese Empire, while prescribing particular permitted languages for calls abroad. Foreign-language calls within a city remain possible, but English cannot presently be used between the Embassy and consular offices. Code telegrams sent abroad must be accompanied by translations unless they are official government messages.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 413 authorizing a protest
subfiles.about: Authorizes the Embassy to protest if the prohibition on English seriously impairs American diplomatic and consular work.
subfiles.summary: The Department authorizes a protest based on the operational necessity of English-language communications between the Embassy, consulates, and American citizens in Japan. It argues that the restriction impairs American representation and conflicts with reciprocal permission for diplomatic and consular establishments to function. Although the form bears a July 16 preparation date, later telegrams consistently identify this instruction as no. 413 of July 19.

subfiles.title: Langdon memorandum on European precedents
subfiles.to: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.about: Reviews European precedents for restrictions on foreign-language telephone and telegraph communications.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum notes temporary prohibitions on non-Spanish telephone conversations during battle or siege conditions in the Spanish Civil War and temporary restrictions during the Warsaw campaign. It states that Germany otherwise allowed American representatives to use English and that British restrictions concerned coded telegrams rather than spoken language. Langdon concludes that there is no European precedent requiring acquiescence in Japan’s proposed restriction.

subfiles.title: Notification to the Federal Communications Commission
subfiles.about: Forwards the July 14 Tokyo telegram concerning Japan’s new telecommunications regulations.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary of State sends the Federal Communications Commission a copy of Grew’s July 14 telegram. The letter is informational and contains no request for action beyond bringing the Japanese regulations to the Commission’s attention.

subfiles.title: Telegram from Grew on the initial approach to the Foreign Office
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador in Japan
subfiles.about: Reports that the Embassy raised the English-language prohibition with the Japanese Foreign Office but considered further protest likely futile.
subfiles.summary: Grew says the prohibition seriously interferes with communications among the Embassy and consulates, especially on the Tokyo–Yokohama and Kobe–Osaka routes. The Embassy invoked reciprocity, but the Foreign Office replied that Japanese residents in the United States would suffer less under comparable restrictions because most spoke English. Grew therefore initially judged additional representations unlikely to succeed.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 461 directing a formal protest
subfiles.about: Directs the Embassy to make a formal protest and obtain a prompt official Japanese reply.
subfiles.summary: The Department rejects the idea that the matter should be dropped as futile and instructs the Embassy to protest formally along the lines previously authorized. The Foreign Office is to be told that the United States expects a prompt formal reply for governmental consideration. The form bears a July 30 preparation date, while subsequent correspondence identifies the transmitted instruction as no. 461 of August 2.

subfiles.title: Telegram reporting delivery of Grew’s protest note
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador in Japan
subfiles.about: Reports that Grew delivered a first-person protest note to the Japanese Minister for Foreign Affairs.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports that he addressed a first-person note to the Minister for Foreign Affairs on August 5. The note followed the Department’s instruction to protest the telephone regulations formally.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 1287 on the Japanese explanation
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador in Japan
subfiles.about: Reports the Japanese Foreign Minister’s claim that the restrictions resulted from similar British regulations.
subfiles.summary: The Foreign Minister raises the American protest and apologizes for the delay in providing satisfaction, claiming that Japan acted because comparable restrictions existed in Great Britain. Grew calls it illogical to penalize Americans for British measures. The Minister says he intends to discuss the matter with the British Ambassador in search of a solution.

subfiles.title: Duplicate copy of telegram no. 1287
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador in Japan
subfiles.about: Duplicate received copy of Grew’s report on Japan’s attempt to justify its telephone restrictions by reference to British policy.
subfiles.summary: This copy repeats Grew’s account of the Foreign Minister’s explanation that the Japanese rules followed purported British restrictions. It also repeats Grew’s rejection of that reasoning and the Minister’s proposal to consult the British Ambassador. Its receipt notation differs from that on the preceding copy.

subfiles.title: Inquiry to London about British telephone regulations
subfiles.about: Asks whether Great Britain prohibits Japanese officials from speaking Japanese in domestic telephone conversations.
subfiles.summary: The Department relays the Japanese Foreign Minister’s assertion that Japan’s regulations were based on similar British measures. London is asked to verify whether any prohibition exists and, if so, to provide its enforcement date and the nature of the restrictions.

subfiles.title: Winant telegram denying a British domestic-language prohibition
subfiles.from: John G. Winant, U.S. Ambassador to the United Kingdom
subfiles.about: Reports the British Foreign Office’s denial that domestic telephone conversations are restricted by language.
subfiles.summary: Winant reports that the British Foreign Office emphatically denies any prohibition on Japanese or any other language in telephone conversations within Great Britain. English is required only for overseas telephone calls. The response was also telegraphed to Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Telegram to Tokyo rebutting the British justification
subfiles.from: Cordell Hull, U.S. Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Instructs Grew to press Japan for a formal reply after Britain denies having comparable domestic restrictions.
subfiles.summary: The Department informs Tokyo that the British Foreign Office emphatically denies restricting the use of Japanese or other languages in domestic telephone calls, although English is required for overseas calls. It adds that British measures would not in any case justify denying American officials an essential facility in Japan. Grew is told to press the Japanese Government for a prompt formal response to his protest.

subfiles.title: Telegram announcing restoration of foreign-language telephone calls
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador in Japan
subfiles.about: Reports the Japanese Foreign Office’s announcement that foreign-language telephone conversations had again been permitted.
subfiles.summary: A September 16 Foreign Office note verbale states that telephone conversations in foreign languages had been permitted from the evening of September 13. Grew confirms the practical effect by reporting that the Embassy Counselor spoke in English by telephone with the Consul General at Yokohama.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 5795 transmitting Grew’s protest note
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador in Japan
subfiles.about: Transmits a copy of Grew’s August 5 formal protest against restrictions on English-language telephone communications.
subfiles.summary: Grew supplements his August 5 telegram by forwarding the complete text of note no. 1870 to the Minister for Foreign Affairs. The despatch identifies the note as the formal protest made pursuant to the Department’s instruction no. 461.

subfiles.title: Enclosure: Grew’s note no. 1870 to Admiral Toyoda
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador in Japan
subfiles.to: Admiral Teijiro Toyoda, Japanese Minister for Foreign Affairs
subfiles.about: Formally protests Japan’s prohibition on English-language telephone communications and requests a prompt reply.
subfiles.summary: Grew argues that English is essential for communications among the Embassy, consulates, and citizens residing in Japan and that the prohibition impairs the representation of American interests. He characterizes it as contrary to the reciprocal permission granted by the United States and Japan for their diplomatic and consular establishments. Acting on instructions, he requests a prompt formal reply; a copy was also sent to the British Embassy.

interest: The file offers a compact case study of how an apparently technical telecommunications rule became a significant diplomatic issue during the deterioration of U.S.–Japanese relations in 1941. Its successive telegrams preserve the full escalation from reporting and informal representations to a formal protest, international fact-checking through London, and eventual Japanese retreat. Particularly useful are the internal memorandum on European wartime precedents, the duplicate copies with differing receipt markings, and the complete text of Grew’s protest, which together illuminate State Department reasoning, communications procedures, and the practical dependence of diplomacy on ordinary infrastructure.
